title: वर्णानामुुच्चारणस्थानसमीक्षा
nepali: प्रस्तुुतोऽयं लेखो देवनागरीवर्णेष्वाचार्येण पाणिनिना कृतस्य स्थानविभागस्य समुल्लेखने तत्राधुुनिकैर्वैयाकरणैः कृतस्य परिष्कारस्य समीक्षणे च केन्द्रितो वर्तते । एतत्क्रमे लेखोऽयं प्रथमत आचार्येण पाणिनिना निर्धारितानि स्थानानि समुल्लिख्य तत्राधुनिकानां मतानि समीक्षते । अतोऽत्र स्थाननिर्धारणविषये प्राचीनाचार्र्यैः कृतो विभागः कीदृशोऽस्ति ? तत्रार्वाचीनैः कृतपरिष्कारश्च कीदृगस्तीति शोधप्रश्नं कृत्वा तस्योत्तरं दत्तमस्ति । अनयोः समस्ययोः समाधानायात्र पुुस्तकालयतः सम्बद्धाः सामग्रीर्गृृहीत्वा वर्णनात्मक–विश्लेषणात्मक–विवेचनात्मकैर्विधिभिस्तथ्याङ्कानां विश्लेषण– मूहापोहनञ्च विधाय निष्कर्षो निष्पादितो वर्तते । विषयविश्लेषणक्रमे संस्कृतव्याकरणे प्रसिद्धस्य निर्वचनविधेः प्रयोगोऽपि यथास्थानं विहितोऽस्ति । तिष्ठति यत्र वर्णोत्पादको वायुस्तत् स्थानमिति व्युत्पत्त्या फुस्फुसातो निसृतो वायुुः प्रथमं यत्रावरुध्यते स्पृशति वा तदेव स्थानम्, अतो वायोः प्रथमगत्यवरोधस्थानं हि वास्तविकमुुच्चारणस्थानमिति निश्चीयते । वर्णानां स्थानमिति शास्त्रीयव्यवहारस्तु औपचारिक एव, न तु वास्तविक इति सर्वैैरवगन्तव्यम् । वायोर्विकारो वर्ण इति वाक्यपदीयसिद्धान्ताद् वायोर्विशेषकम्पनम्, शब्दाद्युच्चारणापेक्षया वायोर्बहिरागमनं तन्मध्ये कण्ठताल्वादिष्वभिघात एव वर्णोच्चारणप्रक्रियेति शास्त्रीयं मतम् । देवनागरीवर्णानां स्थानविभाजनपरम्परा वैदिकव्याकरणतः प्रारब्धा दृश्यते । एतादृशं विभाजनं प्रथमत ऋक्प्रातिशाख्येन प्रारब्धं ततः सामाथर्वयजुरादिभिस्तैत्तिरीयादिभिश्च प्रातिशाख्यैः कृतं दृश्यते। प्रातिशाख्यव्याकरणैः कृतं विभाजनमाश्रित्य लौकिकैर्वैयाकरणैरिन्द्रचान्द्रादिभिः तानाश्रित्याचार्येण पाणिनिना कृतं दृश्यते । ततः पाणिनीयपरम्परानुयायिभिरनेकैः संस्कृतवैयाकरणैः स्थानानि विभक्तानि । तत्र पूर्ववत्र्तीनि स्थूलविभाजनानि क्रमशः सूूक्ष्मीकृत्य कुत्रचित् संशोध्य च पाणिनीयशिक्षाकारेण– अष्टौ स्थानानि वर्णानामुरः कण्ठः शिरस्तथा, जिह्वामूलं च दन्ताश्च नासिकोष्ठौ च तालु च प्रभृतिभिः शिक्षावाक्यैर्वर्णानां स्थानानि निर्धारितानि, तत्क्रमे नासिकाऽपि स्थाने गृहीता । पाणिनीयशिक्षायां कृतः स स्थानविभागः तदुत्तरवत्र्तिभिः पतञ्जलि–काशिकाकार–नागेश–कैयट–भट्टोजिदीक्षित–प्रक्रियाकौमुदीकृद्भिः विनापरिवर्तनेन समर्थितः । गच्छता काले पाणिनीयशिक्षायां निर्धारितानि तानि स्थानानि पाश्चाŒयमतावलम्बिभिर्नैपालैर्भारतीयैश्चाधुनिकैर्भाषाविद्भिराधुनिकैध्र्वनिरुपकरणैः परीक्ष्य किञ्चित् संशोधितानि । एतत्क्रमे कण्ठ्यस्थानतो हकारो, तालव्यस्थानत इचुशाः, मूर्धा÷वत्स्र्यस्थानत ऋकारः, दन्त्यस्थानत लृनलसास्तथा ओष्ठ्यस्थानत उकारश्च निष्कासिताः पुनः स्वरयन्त्रमुखे हकार, वत्स्र्यस्थाने चवर्गनकारलकारसकाराः, ओष्ठ्ये वकारश्च विन्यस्तः । अथर्वप्रातिशाख्ये–नासिक्यवर्णानां नासिकास्थानं नासिकैव करणमित्युक्तमासीत् परमाधुनिकैरेतेषां वर्णानामस्यबहिर्भूतत्वं मत्वा करणत्वं स्वीकृतम् । विभिन्नेषु प्रातिशाख्येषु पाणिनीयशिक्षादिषुु च कृतः स्थानविभागस्तात्कालिकानां तद्देशीयानां तज्जातीयानाञ्चोच्चारणानुकूल आसीत्, तदानीमपि प्राच्योदीच्यादिषु देशेषूच्चारणभेद आसीदिति एङ्प्राचां देशे (पा.सू.१–१–७५), उदीचामातः स्थाने एकपूर्वायाः (पा.सू.७–३–४६) प्रभृतिभिः पाणिनीयसूत्रैरवगम्यते । एतेन तात्कालिकी संस्कृतभाषा भरतखण्डे प्रसृता वाग्व्यवहारे प्रयुुक्ता गातिशीला चासीदित्यप्यनुुमीयते । भाषा गतिशीला भवतीति पक्षेऽथवा महाभारतोत्तरकालाद् वर्णानामुुच्चारणपद्धतिः क्रमशः क्षयं गतेति पक्षेऽपि वर्णानामुच्चारणपद्धतिः किञ्चिद् परिवर्तिता इति सर्वैः स्वीकृता दृश्यते, एतेन कालान्तरेण देशान्तरेण वा वर्णानां पूर्वनिर्दिष्टमुुच्चारणस्थानं वा तत्सम्बद्धा धारणा परिवर्तितुुं शक्नोतीति मन्तव्यम्, प्राचीनैरन्तः साक्ष्येण पुनः पुुनरुच्चारणेन कृते विभागेऽर्वाचीनैध्र्वनिसंयन्त्रैः सूूक्ष्मतरेण परीक्षणेन कृतो वर्तते, अतः पूर्वनिर्धारणे जातं परिवर्तनं स्वाभाविकं मन्तव्यमिति लेखसारः ।
american_english: This presented article focuses on elucidating the classification of places of articulation of Devanagari phonemes made by Acarya Panini and on reviewing the refinements made therein by modern grammarians. In this sequence, this article first articulates the places determined by Acarya Panini and then examines the opinions of modern scholars thereon. Therefore, what is the classification made by ancient acharyas regarding the determination of places of articulation here? And framing the research question of what kind of refinement has been made therein by modern scholars, its answer has been provided. To resolve these two problems, relevant materials were obtained from the library, and conclusions have been drawn by analyzing and thoroughly examining the data through descriptive, analytical, and evaluative methods. In the process of analyzing the subject matter, the etymological method renowned in Sanskrit grammar has also been employed where appropriate. Based on the etymology that 'that place where the sound-producing air resides is the sthana (place of articulation),' the very place where the air expelled from the lungs is first obstructed or makes contact is indeed the sthana; therefore, the place of the air's first obstruction of movement is determined to be the actual place of articulation. It should be understood by all that the scholarly usage 'place of phonemes' is merely formal, not literal. Based on the doctrine of the Vakyapadiya that 'phoneme is a modification of air,' the scholarly view holds that the process of phoneme pronunciation consists of the specific vibration of air, the outward expulsion of air required for uttering words, and meanwhile the striking against the throat, palate, and other organs. The tradition of classifying the places of articulation of Devanagari phonemes is seen to have originated from Vedic grammar. Such a division is seen to have been initiated first by the Rk-Pratisakhya and subsequently carried out by the Sama, Atharva, Yajur, Taittiriya, and other Pratisakhyas. Drawing upon the classification made by the Pratisakhya grammars, classical grammarians such as Indra and Candra, and drawing upon them Acarya Panini, are seen to have developed it. Thereafter, the places of articulation were classified by numerous Sanskrit grammarians following the Paninian tradition. Therein, gradually refining earlier coarse divisions and amending them in places, the author of the Paniniya-Siksa determined the places of phonemes through instructional verses such as 'Eight are the places of phonemes: chest, throat, head, tongue-root, teeth, nose, lips, and palate,' and in that sequence, the nose was also accepted as a place of articulation. That division of places established in the Paniniya-Siksa was endorsed without alteration by subsequent authorities: Patanjali, the authors of the Kasika, Nagesa, Kaiyata, Bhattoji Diksita, and the author of the Prakriya-Kaumudi. Over time, those places determined in the Paniniya-Siksa were tested with modern phonetic equipment and slightly revised by modern Nepali and Indian linguists who followed Western views. In this process, the 'h' sound was removed from the velar place, 'i', the 'c'-series, and 's' from the palatal place, the vowel 'r' from the retroflex/alveolar place, 'lr', 'n', 'l', and 's' from the dental place, and the vowel 'u' from the labial place; furthermore, 'h' was reassigned to the glottis, the 'c'-series, 'n', 'l', and 's' to the alveolar place, and 'v' to the labial place. In the Atharva-Pratisakhya, it was stated that for nasal phonemes the nose is the place and the nose itself is the articulator, but modern scholars, considering these phonemes to fall outside the mouth cavity, have accepted it as an articulator. The division of places made across various Pratisakhyas and the Paniniya-Siksa suited the pronunciation of the people of that time, region, and community, and even then there were regional variations in pronunciation between eastern and northern lands, as understood from Paninian sutras such as 'en pracam dese' (Panini 1.1.75) and 'udicam atah sthane ekapurvayah' (Panini 7.3.46). From this, it is also inferred that the Sanskrit language of that period was widespread across Bharatkhanda (the Indian subcontinent), actively used in speech, and dynamic. Whether from the premise that language is dynamic or the premise that the manner of phoneme pronunciation gradually deteriorated after the Mahabharata era, it is seen to be accepted by all that the pronunciation system of phonemes underwent some change; therefore, it should be recognized that over time or across different regions, the previously specified place of articulation of phonemes or concepts related thereto can change; while the division made by the ancients was based on internal evidence and repeated pronunciation, that made by modern scholars is based on finer testing with acoustic instruments; hence, the changes occurring in earlier determinations should be regarded as natural—such is the summary of the paper.

That division of places established in the Paniniya-Siksa was backed without alteration by subsequent authorities: Patanjali, the authors of the Kasika, Nagesa, Kaiyata, Bhattoji Diksita, and the author of the Prakriya-Kaumudi. Over time, those places determined in the Paniniya-Siksa were tested with modern phonetic equipment and slightly revised by modern Nepali and Indian linguists who followed Western views. In this process, the 'h' sound was removed from the velar place, 'i', the 'c'-series, and 's' from the palatal place, the vowel 'r' from the retroflex/alveolar place, 'lr', 'n', 'l', and 's' from the dental place, and the vowel 'u' from the labial place; furthermore, 'h' was reassigned to the glottis, the 'c'-series, 'n', 'l', and 's' to the alveolar place, and 'v' to the labial place. In the Atharva-Pratisakhya, it was stated that for nasal phonemes the nose is the place and the nose itself is the articulator, but modern scholars, considering these phonemes to fall outside the mouth cavity, have accepted it as an articulator. The division of places made across various Pratisakhyas and the Paniniya-Siksa suited the pronunciation of the people of that time, region, and community, and even then there were regional variations in pronunciation between eastern and northern lands, as understood from Paninian sutras such as 'en pracam dese' (Panini 1.1.75) and 'udicam atah sthane ekapurvayah' (Panini 7.3.46). From this, it is also inferred that the Sanskrit language of that period was widespread across Bharatkhanda (the Indian subcontinent), actively used in speech, and dynamic. Whether from the premise that language is dynamic or the premise that the manner of phoneme pronunciation gradually deteriorated after the Mahabharata era, it is seen to be accepted by all that the pronunciation system of phonemes underwent some change; therefore, it should be recognized that over time or across different regions, the previously specified place of articulation of phonemes or concepts related thereto can change; while the division made by the ancients was based on internal evidence and repeated pronunciation, that made by modern scholars is based on finer testing with acoustic instruments; hence, the changes occurring in earlier determinations should be regarded as natural—such is the summary of the paper.
